heading.en: From frequency back to voice, and from voice to pulses

hook.en: An FM detector must turn frequency changes into voltage changes. And your phone does something stranger still: it chops your voice into thousands of samples every second and sends numbers.

narration.en: An FM detector must turn frequency changes into voltage changes. And your phone does something stranger still: it chops your voice into thousands of samples every second and sends numbers.

body.en: An FM detector (discriminator) produces an output voltage proportional to the frequency deviation. The simple slope detector tunes an LC circuit slightly off the carrier, so that frequency changes move along the sloping side of its response and become amplitude changes, which a diode detector then recovers. Better circuits are the Foster–Seeley discriminator, the ratio detector (which also rejects amplitude noise) and the phase-locked loop (PLL). A limiter before the detector removes amplitude variations.

points.en: Slope detector: FM → AM → diode detector
Limiter removes amplitude noise before detection

narration.en: An FM detector turns frequency changes into voltage changes. The slope detector uses the sloping side of a tuned circuit; the ratio detector and PLL are better versions.
narration.kn: FM ಡಿಟೆಕ್ಟರ್ ಆವೃತ್ತಿಯ ಬದಲಾವಣೆಯನ್ನು ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್ ಆಗಿ ಬದಲಿಸುತ್ತದೆ. ಸ್ಲೋಪ್ ಡಿಟೆಕ್ಟರ್ ಟ್ಯೂನ್ಡ್ ಮಂಡಲದ ಇಳಿಜಾರನ್ನು ಬಳಸುತ್ತದೆ.

title.en: On the board: Slope detection and sampling

say.en: A slope detector tunes an LC circuit a little away from the carrier, so the carrier sits on the sloping side of the response.
Now a change of frequency becomes a change of amplitude, and an ordinary diode detector recovers the audio.
Better circuits are the Foster-Seeley discriminator, the ratio detector and the phase-locked loop, with a limiter in front.
In pulse modulation we send samples. Taking samples often enough keeps all the information of the message.
The sampling theorem: sample at least twice the highest message frequency. In PCM each sample becomes an n-bit code.
Example: a 5 kilohertz message needs at least 10 kilohertz sampling. With 8 bits, that is 256 levels and 80 kilobits per second.

body.en: In pulse modulation the carrier is a train of pulses. The sampling theorem says a signal with highest frequency $f_m$ is fully described by samples taken at $f_s \ge 2f_m$ (the Nyquist rate). In PAM the pulse amplitude follows the message, in PWM the pulse width, and in PPM the pulse position. In PCM each sample is quantised to one of $2^n$ levels and sent as an n-bit binary code, giving a bit rate of $n f_s$. Digital carriers are keyed as ASK, FSK or PSK.

points.en: PAM / PWM / PPM: amplitude / width / position
ASK, FSK, PSK for digital data

narration.en: Sample at least twice the highest message frequency. PAM, PWM and PPM vary the pulse amplitude, width and position; PCM sends each sample as an n-bit code.
narration.kn: ಅತಿ ಹೆಚ್ಚು ಸಂದೇಶ ಆವೃತ್ತಿಯ ಕನಿಷ್ಠ ಎರಡರಷ್ಟು ದರದಲ್ಲಿ ಮಾದರಿ ತೆಗೆಯಬೇಕು. PAM, PWM, PPM ಪಲ್ಸ್‌ನ ವೈಶಾಲ್ಯ, ಅಗಲ, ಸ್ಥಾನವನ್ನು ಬದಲಿಸುತ್ತವೆ; PCM ಪ್ರತಿ ಮಾದರಿಯನ್ನು n-ಬಿಟ್ ಸಂಕೇತವಾಗಿ ಕಳುಹಿಸುತ್ತದೆ.

tryThis.en: Set fm = 4 kHz, fs = 8 kHz, n = 8: the 64 kbit/s telephone channel.
Lower fs below 2fm: the ratio drops under 1 and the message cannot be rebuilt.
Each extra bit doubles the number of levels.

problem.en: A telephone voice channel extends to 3.4 kHz. It is sampled at 8 kHz and each sample is coded with 8 bits. (a) Is the sampling rate adequate? (b) How many quantisation levels? (c) Bit rate?

steps.en: (a) Nyquist rate = 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 kHz; 8 kHz > 6.8 kHz, so it is adequate.
